catalog_quote: All Shiwiar words exhibit a prosodic prominence which I have labelled as accent in this work. In many ways, it resembles what has been analysed as stress for other languages; but in one regard it also exhibits typical tonal qualities. ... As would be typical for a stress system, every phonological word in Shiwiar only has one primary accent which is usually associated with a single vowel, as in (5.184). This is manifested phonetically by higher pitch, longer duration and increased amplitude compared to other vowels in the word. ... Accent placement in Shiwiar is not predictable based on general phonotactic or metric principles. Even the claim that accent is lexically specified (i.e. that each word has an accent on a particular syllable) is hard to uphold because there is so much variation – both in the speech of a single person and across speakers. It is therefore difficult to make generalisations, but there are certain tendencies that should be noted. In nouns, the accent is typically associated with a vowel in the root, as in (5.186), but a limited number of suffixes tend to attract accent instead, as in (5.187). ... The addition of nominal suffixes and clitics often triggers a rightward shift in accent placement in nouns. ... Compounds and noun phrases have a strong tendency to be accented on the last vowel of the first word, even if that is not the vowel that is normally accented in those words in isolation.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word carries exactly one primary accent (culminative; realised by pitch, duration and intensity, with tone-like rightward spreading of high pitch under some suffixes such as the vocative). Its position is not derivable from syllable count, weight or any metrical principle and is at best lexically/morphologically determined with considerable free variation: nouns tend to accent a root vowel, certain suffixes attract the accent, adding nominal suffixes/enclitics often shifts the accent one vowel rightward (júmi 'water' vs jumí=nʲ), and accent shift alone can mark case (íkʲam 'forest' vs ikʲám LOC). Fast's SIL descriptions of Peruvian Achual/Corrientes Jívaro (1975, DEL 20 p. 9; DEL 21 p. 3; 1974 annex) independently state that accent is phonemic, give minimal pairs (núŋka 'tierra' vs nuŋká 'en la tierra', wári 'rápido' vs warí '¿qué?'), and say explicitly 'no hay regla para prever dónde debe caer el énfasis'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Kohlberger: only one primary accent per phonological word; no secondary stress described, but the accent's high pitch can spread over all following vowels in certain morphological configurations (e.g. vocative umát͡ʃírú). Fast 1975 (DEL 21 p. 18; DEL 20 sec. 3.3): a secondary accent exists, sometimes as strong as the primary and distinguished from it by (lower) tone; its position is not predictable.
new_statements.exceptions: Tendencies rather than rules: a limited set of suffixes attract accent; in verbs either root or certain suffixes bear it; compounds and whole noun phrases form one accent domain and strongly tend to be accented on the last vowel of the first word even when that vowel is unaccented in isolation (hápa 'red brocket' vs hapá_jãwãã 'cougar'); reduplications accent the last vowel of the first copy; monosyllabic roots double their vowel in isolation. Accent shift marks locative/genitive on some nouns and vocative (Fast dictionary: vocative = accent on last syllable).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including enclitics; compounds and noun phrases count as a single accent domain with one accent. Kohlberger describes the Shiwiar variety (Ecuador, Conambo/Corrientes basin); Fast describes Peruvian Achual (Huasaga) and Corrientes-river Jívaro; all fall under Glottolog achu1248 / ISO acu, and all agree that accent is contrastive and not positionally fixed.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog achu1248 / ISO acu lumps Achuar and Shiwiar (Kohlberger 2020: 22 fn. c notes this explicitly and treats them as distinct varieties). The quoted modern statement (Kohlberger 2020) describes Shiwiar as spoken in Juyuintsa and other Ecuadorian Shiwiar villages (Conambo/Corrientes basin). The SIL sources describe Peruvian varieties: Fast 1975 DEL 20 = 'achual' of the Río Huasaga (Loreto), Fast 1975 DEL 21 = 'jíbaro del río Corrientes' (1961-62 data, ~500 speakers, Arboleda), both catalogued by SIL/Glottolog under acu/achu1248. All three agree: contrastive (phonemic) accent, one per word, position not predictable by rule.

new_statements.translation: p. 16: "The orthographic accent, in some cases, is the only thing that distinguishes the meaning of two words, for example: kúchi 'pig'; kuchí 'knife'." — p. 27: "Note that the vocative, which is the case used to call or address a person, is distinguished from the genitive in that the accent falls on the last syllable." — p. 28: "It should be noted that besides adding the person suffix, the accent sometimes falls on the following syllable. In some examples, possession is indicated only by the change of accent; for example: núwe clay / nuwé his/her clay; súwe throat / suwé his/her throat [...] Note in the last example that in the monosyllabic form jée the accent does not change."

new_statements.rule_in_words: The dictionary gives no placement rule. It marks the accent orthographically on whichever syllable carries it (ája, ajár, ajáram, ajári; múuk, múukur, múukem, muuké; yatsúr, yatsúru; yawáa, tirángkur), states that accent alone can distinguish word meaning (kúchi 'pig' vs kuchí 'knife'), that the vocative differs from the genitive by accent on the final syllable (yatsúru 'of my brother' vs yatsurú 'brother!'), and that possessive suffixation often shifts the accent one syllable rightward, sometimes being the sole exponent of possession (núwe/nuwé), but not in monosyllables (jée). This is lexically contrastive, morphologically mobile accent with no fixed position.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic stems keep their accent under possession (jée 'his/her house'); the rightward shift under possessive suffixes happens 'a veces' (sometimes), not always (ajár, ajáram, ajári keep the stem accent; muuké shifts).
new_statements.identity_note: Work 2 (the dictionary) describes Peruvian Achuar-Shiwiar and lists five river dialects (Anasu, Corrientes, Huasaga, Huitoyacu, Puranchim); the catalog's existing statement (Kohlberger 2020) describes Shiwiar as spoken in Ecuador (Pastaza). Work 0/1 (Fast & Fast 1981) is a pedagogical grammar of Peruvian Achuar. All are treated under achu1248 by Glottolog.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The book (a pedagogical introduction, not a full grammar) never states where word accent falls. It treats accent as contrastive: the practical orthography marks it only where it alone distinguishes two words, and the lessons mark it on almost every word so the learner can place it. Accent also moves under morphology: disyllabic noun stems shift accent between the subject form and the object/stem form (úchi / uchín / uchí-), and the vocative of proper names puts the accent on the added -á / -iá. No dedicated accent section; the three passages quoted are the whole of what it says.
new_statements.exceptions: Morphologically conditioned accent shifts only: disyllabic stems change accent between subject and direct-object/stem forms (p. 42); vocative of proper names accents the added -á/-iá (p. 88). No default placement, no weight statement, no exceptions list.
new_statements.identity_note: Fast & Fast 1981 describes Peruvian Achuar ('unos tres mil nativos.. entre los ríos Morona, por el oeste y Tigre por el este', p. 11), noting minor dialect differences in pronunciation that the book ignores; the catalog record rests on Kohlberger 2020's Shiwiar of Ecuador. Both varieties sit under glottocode achu1248 (Achuar-Shiwiar).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Kohlberger 2020 statement (one primary accent per phonological word, catalogued as lexical/unpredictable): Fast & Fast treat accent as meaning-distinguishing and learner-unpredictable and show morphologically conditioned accent shifts, with no fixed-position rule. It adds the detail that accent alternates within noun paradigms (subject vs. object form) and that vocative -á/-iá is accent-bearing, but gives no phonological placement rule, so it neither refines the placement nor contradicts it. Note the variety differs: this is Peruvian Achuar (Morona-Tigre), not Ecuadorian Shiwiar as in Kohlberger.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A pedagogical grammar with no lesson or rule on accent placement. It treats accent as contrastive (the practical orthography marks it only where it distinguishes two words, and the book marks it on nearly every word because the learner cannot predict it), and shows accent alternating with morphology: disyllabic noun radicals carry initial accent in the bare subject form but non-initial accent in the object form and the bound radical (úchi / uchín / uchí-), and the vocative suffix -á/-iá attracts the accent. Accent marks throughout the examples fall on varying syllables (kurámak, nuwáp, tutáng, chíngki, wéjmak, japímuk, sungkúr), i.e. not a fixed position.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent shift in two-syllable radicals between subject and object/radical forms (p. 42); vocative -á/-iá takes the accent with proper names (p. 88). Introduction (p. 11) notes dialect differences in pronunciation (e.g. voiceless final vowels in one dialect) that the book ignores.
new_statements.identity_note: Fast & Fast 1981 describes Peruvian Achuar spoken between the Morona and Tigre rivers in northern Peru (p. 11), and explicitly sets aside dialect differences in pronunciation; the existing catalog statement (Kohlberger 2020) describes Shiwiar of Ecuador. Both fall under glottocode achu1248 (Achuar-Shiwiar).
